story831:
In the beginning, before the world took shape, there were only four seas surrounding a floating island in the First World — Ni' Hodiłhił, the Black World. This was a place of darkness and mist, where the Air-Spirit People drifted like thoughts尚未 given form, and the insect people crawled through shadows that had no source.

First Woman — Áłtsé Asdzą́ą́ — was formed from the meeting of clouds and wind in the East, her body woven from vapor and breath. First Man — Áłtsé Hastiin — arose the same way in the West, carrying white corn in one hand and crystal in the other. They had never seen each other, but each could see the glow of the other's fire across the dark waters.

First Woman struck turquoise and made a fire. First Man struck crystal and made his own. When they saw each other's light reflecting off the four seas, they walked toward it. But Great Coyote — Mąʼiitoʼí Áłchíní — appeared between them, claiming he knew everything beneath the water and above the sky, and he walked with them as they joined.

Then came First Angry — Áłtsé Hashké — who claimed he had been there before all of them and brought with him the knowledge of witchcraft and discord. Wherever he walked, the air thickened. Conflict erupted among the Air-Spirit People. Brother turned against brother, and the four rulers of the seas could no longer keep order.

The Holy People decided to leave. They climbed upward through a passage in the sky and entered the Second World — Ni' Hodootłʼizh, the Blue World. There, blue-gray mammals roamed under a pale sky, and the Swallow People nested in cliffs that shimmered like frozen rain. But conflict followed them here too, for First Angry could not be left behind. And so, world after world, the Holy People climbed — through the Yellow World of two crossing rivers and six sacred mountains, where the great monsters still roamed, and finally, through the Reed of Emergence, into the White World, the Fourth World, where the sun would rise and the land would take its final shape.

Each world they left behind was not destroyed but folded into the one above, like layers of a prayer hidden inside the next. And when they stepped into the Fourth World at last, the wind hit their faces, and they knew this was where they would remain.
story832:
When the Holy People emerged into the Fourth World, they found it vast and empty, the land stretching in every direction beneath a sky that had no sun. Among them walked White Shell Girl — Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ — born in the Third World from the foam of sacred waters and the breath of First Man. She was quiet where others were loud, still where others moved, and the Holy People sometimes forgot she was there.

But the Sun did not forget.

Turquoise Boy — Jóhonaa'éí — watched her from the place where the sun would eventually rise. He loved her from a distance, sending rays of light that warmed her skin and made the white shell of her body glow. When he finally came to her in the form of a handsome young man wrapped in light, she did not flinch. They spent four days together, and when he departed at dawn, she knew she carried new life within her.

The months passed slowly. Changing Woman — for that is what she was becoming — walked among the people, and her belly grew round as the full moon. On the day of her delivery, the earth shook. She gave birth to two boys, each emerging from different sides of her body. The first was Naayéé' Neizghání — Monster Slayer — born from her right side, his fists already clenched around bolts of lightning. The second was Tóbájíshchíní — Child of the Water — born from her left, his eyes reflecting the depth of every lake and river.

The twins grew with unnatural speed. Within days they were walking, within weeks they were men, and within months they had set out to destroy the monsters — the anaye — that had been devouring the people since the time of the separation. They killed Yéʼiitsoh, the Big Giant, and Déélgééd the Horned Monster, and all the others who had made the Fourth World a place of terror.

After the monsters fell, Changing Woman grew old. Her skin wrinkled, her hair turned white, and she knew her time in the physical world was ending. But she made a promise: each year, as winter approached, she would age further, until she became nothing but memory. And each spring, when the first warm wind blew from the west, she would be young again.

She built a floating house of turquoise and abalone shell on an island in the western ocean and departed from the shore in a boat of light. The people watched her go. And every year since, when the leaves turn gold and fall, the Navajo know it is Changing Woman growing old. And when the first green shoots push through the soil in spring, they know she has been born again.
story833:
In the First World, before there was a sky or a sun, the air was thick with voices that had no bodies. Black Cloud and White Cloud met in the East, swirling together like two rivers joining. From their breath, a figure took shape — First Man, Áłtsé Hastiin, formed from the meeting of darkness and light. In his hands he carried white corn and a piece of crystal that glowed from within.

In the West, Blue Cloud and Yellow Cloud came together, and from their union emerged First Woman, Áłtsé Asdzą́ą́, carrying yellow corn, white shell, turquoise, and a bundle of yucca fiber. She was formed from different stuff than First Man — softer, more yielding, but no less powerful.

Neither knew the other existed. First Woman made a fire with turquoise and copper, and the light of it burned blue and steady. First Man struck his crystal against a rock and made a fire of white light. Across the dark waters of the First World, each saw the other's flame — a point of brightness in an ocean of black.

They walked toward each other. Where they met, the ground became firm.

But before they could speak, Great Coyote appeared — Mąʼiitoʼí Áłchíní — his fur gleaming like starlight. He claimed to have been there since before the beginning, that he knew everything hidden beneath the water and everything that would ever happen above it. Whether this was true, no one could say, for Coyote was both the wisest and the most unreliable of all beings.

Then came First Angry, Áłtsé Hashké, who looked at First Man and First Woman and said, "I was here before you. I am the eldest." He brought with him the knowledge of witchcraft — the ability to curse, to deceive, to sow discord among the Air-Spirit People. Where First Angry walked, arguments erupted. Where he spoke, friendships dissolved.

The Holy People gathered and made a decision: they could not remain in the First World with First Angry among them. They found a passage upward and climbed into the Second World. But First Angry followed. He always followed.

It was only when they reached the Fourth World — the White World, the final world — and the monsters were slain, and Changing Woman departed, that First Man and First Woman at last found peace. They settled on the mountain called Torch Mountain, where their fires still burn, and from there they watch over the people they helped bring into being.
story834:
In the Third World, where two rivers crossed and the sacred mountains had not yet been placed, Spider Woman and Spider Man lived near the Crossing of the Waters. They were ancient beings, older than memory, and they knew things that the other Holy People had not yet learned.

Spider Man had shaped a spindle wheel from a flat stone and a piece of cedar. He planted cotton seeds in the dark earth near the riverbank and watched them grow into tall green stalks burred with white fiber. When the cotton was ready, he showed the people how to pull the fibers apart, twist them into thread, and wind them onto the spindle. The thread was fine as spider silk but strong as a river current.

First Woman watched and declared, "Spinning must be done toward the body. That is how beautiful things are drawn into the world — toward us, not away." And so it was decided: the thread would be wound toward the spinner, pulling beauty closer.

Spider Man named the spindle 'turning around with beautiful goods.' Spider Woman, who saw things differently, called it 'turning around with mixed chips,' for she knew that beauty always comes mixed with hardship.

Together they built a rectangular loom frame from four straight poles of juniper. They stretched the warp threads — the long, vertical threads that give the fabric its structure — and showed the people how to pass the weft — the horizontal threads — over and under, over and under, until the cloth appeared like a pattern of the world itself.

Spider Woman taught the colors: white for the East and dawn, turquoise for the South and midday, yellow for the West and twilight, black for the North and night. She showed how to dye the thread with minerals and plants — blue from wild onions, yellow from rabbit brush, red from alder bark.

When the people had learned, Spider Man gave his final instruction: "When a girl is born, rub spider web on her hands and her arms. She will weave without tiring, and her patterns will be true." And to this day, when a Navajo woman sits at her loom, her fingers moving with a rhythm older than the mountains, she is fulfilling a gift that was given in the Third World, before the sun had a name.
story835:
The quarrel began with pride, as quarrels often do. First Woman stood at the river's edge and boasted to the other women, "We can live without men. I thank my own body for the deer that First Man brings — not him." The words carried across the water like stones thrown into stillness.

First Man heard them. His face darkened. He gathered all the men — and the two hermaphrodite twins who belonged fully to neither side — and led them across the river to the north bank. The women remained on the south. The river became a boundary as sharp as a blade.

For four years, the sexes lived apart. The women tried to sustain themselves. They used bones as substitutes for men, and feathers, and long stones smoothed by the river. Nothing worked. The children that were born from these unnatural acts were wrong — twisted, malformed, monstrous. Owl warned them, flying low over the women's camps: "This is not the way. You are bringing evil into the world." But the women were too proud to listen, and too ashamed to cross the river.

On the other bank, the men fared little better. They used animal livers and tried to make do, but their camps were silent and joyless. The children that were born there were also wrong, and the Holy People saw that the world was being corrupted.

First Man, who had never stopped thinking about First Woman, called across the water. His voice was hoarse from disuse. "Come back," he said. "We were made to be together."

First Woman did not answer immediately. She stood on the south bank, her pride warring with her loneliness. Finally, she called back, "We will come, but on rafts, so that neither side submits to the other."

They met in the middle of the river on rafts of bundled reeds. When they came together again, the harmony returned. The monstrous children who had been born during the separation did not disappear — they became the monsters, the anaye, that would later terrorize the Fourth World until the Hero Twins destroyed them.

The story is told to remind the people: separation breeds monsters. Balance is the way of the world.
story836:
After the men and women reunited, they began crossing the river on rafts of bundled reeds, ferrying people and possessions to the south bank where the sacred mountains waited. One mother and her two daughters missed the last crossing. The sun was going down, and the river was rising.

The women waded in. The water was cold, colder than any water should be, and it pulled at them with hands they could not see. Midway across, something seized the two daughters — Big Water Creature, Tééhoołtsódii, the great spirit of the deep water. He dragged them under. The mother screamed and clawed at the surface, but the girls were gone.

Talking God and Water Sprinkler came to the riverbank. They created two bowls — one of white shell, one of blue — and set them spinning on the water's surface. The spinning bowls bored a hole through the river's skin, revealing an underwater house where Big Water Creature kept his captive children in a dark pool.

First Man and First Woman dove through the opening and rescued the girls. But while they were below, Coyote — First Angry — crept into Big Water Creature's house and stole the creature's own two children, hiding them under his robe.

When Big Water Creature discovered his children gone, he flew into a rage that shook the earth. He called water from every direction — from the springs, from the clouds, from the frozen peaks of the north. The river rose. The plains flooded. Water poured through the valleys like a wall.

The people ran to Sisnaajiní, the Sacred Mountain in the East, its peak white with shell and lightning. They climbed to the top as the water lapped at their feet. First Man planted the Male Reed — a hollow stalk as tall as a man — and called to Woodpecker. Woodpecker hollowed the reed with his beak, drilling a passage from the bottom to the top.

The people climbed inside. They could hear the water rising outside, could feel the reed swaying. One by one, they crawled upward through the hollow stem — First Man, First Woman, the Holy People, and even Coyote with the stolen children still under his arm. They emerged into the Fourth World, gasping in the light, just ahead of the flood that pursued them like a living thing.

Behind them, the Third World drowned. But it was not destroyed — it lives still beneath the waters, a place where the Holy People sometimes return in dreams.
story837:
In the Fourth World, where the land stretched empty and dark, the Holy People gathered to discuss the creation of the sun and moon. The world needed light, and without it, the people would remain in twilight forever.

First Man proposed the plan. First Woman agreed. Great Coyote pretended to agree but was secretly angry that no one had asked his opinion. They summoned Black God — the Fire God — from beneath the earth, where he had been sitting with his fire bundle. Water Sprinkler, House God, and Talking God came as well, forming a council of the most powerful beings.

Turquoise Boy stepped forward. He was young and beautiful, his skin the blue-green of shallow water. "I will become the Sun," he said. "But I demand payment: the lives of every being on earth."

The Holy People were silent. Finally, First Man said, "We cannot pay that price. But if you give yourself freely, the people will honor you with ceremonies and prayers for all time."

Turquoise Boy considered. Then he agreed.

White Shell Girl, quieter and paler, offered to become the Moon. Her price was less — only that the months should be marked by her phases.

The ceremony began. First Man heated a piece of turquoise on a buckskin using Black God's sacred fire. When the turquoise glowed white-hot, Turquoise Boy stepped into it and was consumed. From the ashes rose the Sun — Jóhonaa'éí, 'The One Who Rules the Day' — blazing with a light that made the Holy People shield their eyes.

White Shell Girl entered a piece of white shell and became the Moon — Tłʼéhonaaʼéí, 'The One Who Rules the Night' — pale and silver, casting just enough light to see by.

They established twelve months by counting the Moon's phases. White Shell Girl blew a whistle with twelve holes, and each note marked a turning of the season.

But Coyote, who had been excluded from every decision, grew furious. He had wanted a role in the arrangement, a place of importance. In his anger, he cursed the moon's months so they would not align with the sun's. This is why seasons sometimes come early or late, why frost appears when it should not, and why drought strikes without warning. Coyote's spite broke the perfect order, and the world has been slightly off-balance ever since.
story838:
Death came not with a thunderclap but with a silence. One of the hermaphrodite twins — Nádleeh, the one who belonged to both sides — stopped breathing on the first day of the Sun's journey across the sky. His body lay on the ground like a fallen bird, still warm but empty.

The people gathered around, afraid to touch him. They had never seen death before. Some wept. Some backed away. By evening, they abandoned the body on the ground and walked back to camp, casting glances over their shoulders.

The next morning, a man looked down through the Reed to the Third World below and saw the twin sitting by the river, alive but changed. He had crossed into the world of the dead.

The people argued. Some said death should not be permanent. Others said the twin had chosen to go. Coyote — First Angry — listened to both sides, and then he proposed a test.

They went to Black Water Lake, a pool so dark it seemed to swallow light. Coyote picked up a black rock — heavy, smooth, black as the water itself. "I will throw this into the lake," he said. "If it floats, spirits will return after death and there will be no death. If it sinks, death is permanent."

He threw the rock. It sank without a ripple.

The people cried out. Some begged Coyote to throw another, to try again. But Coyote shook his head. "The decision is made."

Two witnesses who had watched the test died four days later, as if to prove the point. The people learned that looking at the dead is dangerous, that death has its own laws.

Coyote justified his decision with a reasoning that was both cruel and wise: "If no one died, the world would fill with people until there was no room to walk. The old would remain trapped in broken bodies forever. The children who are meant to come could never be born."

The people accepted this, though they wept. And from that day forward, death was part of the world — not as punishment, but as the price of renewal. Each spring, when the grass pushes through the snow, it is because something died in winter to make room for what comes next.
story839:
After the sun and moon had been placed in the sky, the world was divided into day and night, but the night was still too dark. The people stumbled in the blackness, unable to see the trail to the river or the path to the gathering grounds.

First Man called a council. "We must decorate the night sky," he said, "the way a weaver decorates a blanket — with pattern and meaning." He drew a plan in the dirt, marking where each star should go, like a cartographer of heaven.

They gathered pieces of rock-star mica — fragments of luminous stone that glowed with inner light — and carried them to the highest point of the sacred mountain.

Black God went first. He was careful, methodical, placing each star with the precision of a medicine man laying out a sandpainting. He placed the North Star — Sǫʼtsoh — at the center, the fixed point around which all other stars would turn. Then he began placing the stars of the Big Dipper — Náhookǫs bikąʼí — arranging them in a circle around the North Star.

First Man placed additional stars of the Big Dipper, and First Woman placed the Little Dipper — Náhookǫs baʼáádí — on the other side of the sky. They worked in silence, their hands moving through the dark like weavers at a loom.

First Man placed the Pleiades — Dilyéhé — seven stars clustered together like sisters. Black God claimed these represented parts of his own body and tried to move them, but First Man held firm. They placed Orion's belt — called Coyote's Feather — and the Rabbit Tracks, and the countless other stars that the people would use to navigate the seasons.

Coyote grew impatient. He had been watching from the side, excluded from the planning, his contributions ignored. When the remaining mica lay in a blanket waiting to be placed, Coyote grabbed the blanket and flung it into the sky.

Stars scattered in every direction — some in neat lines, some in clusters, some isolated in vast dark spaces. The careful plan was ruined.

This is why the constellations follow patterns but the spaces between them are chaotic. This is why some stars shine brightly while others are barely visible. The Holy People placed the important stars with intention; Coyote filled the rest with impulse and spite.

The people look up at night and see both order and disorder, both the work of careful creators and the signature of a trickster who could not bear to be left out.
story840:
After the people emerged into the Fourth World, the land was featureless — flat and gray, stretching to every horizon without interruption. First Man opened the bundle of dirt he had carried from the Third World, a handful of sacred soil saved during the flood.

"We will re-create the mountains," he said, "the way they were, in their proper places."

He called to First Woman, Water Sprinkler, and Black God, and together they shaped the six sacred mountains from the Third World soil, each one placed in a cardinal or intermediate direction, each one adorned with the materials and spirits of its realm.

In the East, they raised Sisnaajiní — Blanca Peak. They decorated it with white shells, white lightning, and white corn. Dark clouds gathered around its summit for male rain. Rock Crystal Boy and Crystal Girl became its resident spirits, their bodies gleaming like the mountain itself.

In the South, they placed Tsoodził — Mount Taylor. They adorned it with turquoise, dark mist, and animals of every kind. Light clouds drifted around it for female rain. Turquoise Boy and Corn Girl made their home there.

In the West, Dookʼoʼoosłííd — the San Francisco Peaks — received abalone shell and yellow corn. The sun set behind it each evening, painting the sky in colors that mirrored the mountain's adornment.

In the North, Dibé Nitsaa — Hesperus Mountain — was covered with black beads and heavy rain. The winter winds blew from its peak, and the darkness of the longest night seemed to emanate from its slopes.

At each mountain, they created resident deities — beings who would tend the sacred sites and channel the powers of the directions to the people. They placed stones and crystals at each peak, each one a repository of spiritual energy.

Then First Man stood at the center and drew a circle in the dirt. "This is the middle," he said. "The mountains surround it. The people will live here, at the center, protected by the powers of all six directions."

The Holy People blessed the mountains and the land between them. And when the ceremony was complete, the Fourth World had a shape — not flat and featureless anymore, but ringed with sacred peaks that held the world together like the posts of a great lodge.
story841:
Changing Woman gave birth to two sons — Monster Slayer, Naayéé' Neizghání, and Child of the Water, Tóbájíshchíní — fathered by the Sun himself. They were born to rid the world of the anaye, the monsters that had been born during the separation of men and women and that had been devouring the people ever since.

The twins grew with terrifying speed. Within weeks they were hunting with bows made of lightning. But they needed weapons powerful enough to kill beings that ordinary arrows could not wound. They decided to journey to the sky to visit their father, the Sun.

The journey was long and filled with tests. The Sun tried to kill them — not out of cruelty, but to prove their worthiness. He built a sweat lodge of stone knives and heated it until the air inside was white with steam. The twins entered and survived. He laid them on a bed of heated stones that should have burned them to ash. They slept through the night and woke unharmed. He filled the lodge with poisoned smoke that would have killed any mortal. Spider Woman breathed a counter-charm through the smoke holes, and the twins survived that too.

Satisfied, the Sun gave them lightning arrows — shafts of pure energy tipped with flint points that could cut through anything — and armor that gleamed like water. "Go back to the earth," he said, "and destroy the anaye."

Monster Slayer found Yéʼiitsoh, the Big Giant, wearing armor of flint knives on his legs. The Sun had weakened the giant with four strikes, and Monster Slayer finished him — first arrow to break the leg armor, second to shatter it, third through the head, fourth to pin his hair to the ground when he tried to rise.

He and his brother slew Déélgééd the Horned Monster by shooting arrows into its body until it fell into the ocean. They destroyed the giant birds, the cliff-kicker, the monsters of hunger and poverty and cold.

But they did not kill everything. When Old Age, Cold, Poverty, and Hunger begged for their lives, the twins listened to their arguments and allowed them to remain in diminished form. The world needed balance. Without suffering, there would be no appreciation for joy.

The monsters were gone. The people were safe. And the twins returned to the sky, where they still stand as guardians against the darkness.
story842:
Of all the monsters the Hero Twins destroyed, none was more feared than Yéʼiitsoh, the Big Giant. He stood taller than a cottonwood tree, his skin the color of dried blood, and across his legs he wore armor made of flint knives — each blade sharper than a hawk's talon, each one capable of slicing through stone.

The people had tried to fight him. Warriors charged with spears and arrows, and the flint armor shattered their weapons like dry twigs. Yéʼiitsoh laughed as he devoured them, his jaws opening wide enough to swallow a man whole.

The Sun had been watching. From his path across the sky, he struck Yéʼiitsoh four times with bolts of lightning, weakening the giant's armor and slowing his movements. Then the Hero Twins came.

Monster Slayer approached first. He carried a bow of lightning and arrows tipped with flint that could cut through anything — or so he believed. He drew and fired at the giant's leg. The arrow struck the flint armor and shattered into dust.

A second arrow. This one was different — blessed by Spider Woman, its tip made of the same flint as the giant's armor but consecrated with songs of destruction. It struck the leg armor and broke through, sending shards of flint flying. The giant staggered, his leg buckling.

Yéʼiitsoh fell forward, face-down in the dust. Monster Slayer shot a third arrow through the back of his head. Child of the Water shot a fourth through his skull from the other side. The arrows met inside the giant's brain.

But Yéʼiitsoh was not dead yet. Spider Woman's voice came from everywhere and nowhere: "He will rise again if you do not pin him down." Monster Slayer shot a fifth arrow that pinned the giant's hair to the earth. The great body shuddered once and was still.

Rivers of blood flowed from the giant's wounds, carving channels in the earth that would become the arroyos of the Navajo homeland. Monster Slayer took the giant's own stone knife — the one he had used to sharpen his flint armor — and cut off his head.

He carried the head back to the people. It was so large it took four men to lift it. They placed it on a rock outside the village, and for a long time it served as a warning: this is what happens to those who prey upon the people.
story843:
The Horned Monster — Déélgééd — lived in the deep water, in the lightless places where the river met the underground springs. It had a single horn rising from its skull like a tower of bone, and its body was long and serpentine, covered in scales that reflected no light.

People who came near the water disappeared. Fishermen found only their empty canoes, spun in circles by the creature's wake. Children who played at the river's edge were pulled under by currents that had no natural source. The monster's horn broke the surface sometimes — a pale spike cutting through the water like a sail — and those who saw it ran.

Monster Slayer and Child of the Water tracked the creature for seven days, following the trail of missing people and the signs that only the Holy People could read — disturbed water, dead fish floating belly-up, the sour smell of the creature's breath rising from the river in bubbles.

They found its lair in a deep pool beneath a cliff. Monster Slayer shot an arrow into the water. It struck something solid, and the pool erupted. Déélgééd rose from the depths, its horn gleaming, its mouth open wide enough to swallow a horse.

Monster Slayer shot again. The arrow pierced the creature's side, and blood — dark, thick, almost black — gushed into the water. The monster dove, trying to escape, but Child of the Water was waiting underwater. He shot an arrow through the creature's belly from below.

Déélgééd surfaced one last time, thrashing so violently that the waves crested over the banks. Both twins shot arrows into its body — three, four, five — until the creature was pinned to the surface by the sheer number of shafts protruding from its flesh.

The monster died slowly, its great body floating on the water like a fallen tree. Its horn washed ashore weeks later, and the Holy People used it in ceremonies for generations — a reminder that the waters held power, and that power could be dangerous.

The pool where Déélgééd died is said to be deeper than any other body of water in the Fourth World. The people do not fish there. They do not let their children play near its banks. They leave offerings at the water's edge — turquoise and cornmeal — and speak softly when they pass.
story844:
Noqoilpi lived at the base of Chʼóolʼį́ʼí — Great Spruce Mountain — in a house of polished stone where the gambling games never stopped. He was beautiful, charming, and utterly without mercy. His smile could convince anyone to play, and his luck was supernatural — the stones always fell where he wanted them, the sticks always landed in his favor.

People came from every direction to challenge him. Warriors came, certain their skill would triumph. Chiefs came, bringing the wealth of their nations. Young men came, proud and certain. One by one, they played. One by one, they lost.

Noqoilpi took everything. Their horses, their weapons, their clothes. Then he took their freedom. The losers became his servants, building his house, cooking his food, carrying his gambling implements. He enslaved entire nations with nothing but a game of chance and a smile.

The Holy People watched. They saw the people enslaved, saw the wealth of many nations piling up at the base of Chʼóolʼį́ʼí. They decided Noqoilpi had gone too far.

They sent a challenger — a man of no particular appearance, carrying no particular wealth. He walked into Noqoilpi's house and sat down across from the great gambler.

They played the moccasin game. Noqoilpi won the first round. The challenger smiled and played again. He won the second. And the third. And the fourth. Each time, the stakes grew higher. Noqoilpi's confidence wavered. His smile faltered.

In the final round, the challenger won everything — Noqoilpi's wealth, his servants, his house, even the clothes off his back.

Noqoilpi stood naked and defeated. The Holy People commanded him to leave the Navajo world forever. He gathered his gambling sticks and his stones and walked eastward, disappearing over the horizon. He was never seen again.

But his influence lingered. The games he left behind — the moccasin game, the stick game, the guessing games — became part of Navajo life. And the people tell this story to remind themselves: gambling is the vice of Noqoilpi, and those who play too long may lose more than they can afford.
story845:
The animals gathered in a clearing on a cold winter night to play the moccasin game — Yéʼiiʼ — the sacred game that determines the balance between light and dark, summer and winter. The day animals took one side, the night animals the other.

The rules were simple: four moccasins lay in a row on the ground. A small stone — or a ball of yucca fiber — was hidden under one of them. The opposing side had to guess which moccasin held the stone. If they guessed right, they won a point. If they guessed wrong, the hiding side won.

The night animals were winning. The day animals grew desperate. Coyote, who sat among the night animals, saw their distress. He was supposed to help his side, but Coyote's loyalty was always to himself first.

He took a ring of yucca fiber and slipped it under his own moccasin instead of the stone. When the day animals guessed his moccasin, they found only the ring — no stone. They lost the point. Coyote grinned.

But the game went on. The night animals' lead grew. The day animals played harder, drawing on every scrap of cunning they possessed. The moccasins were shuffled, the stone was moved, the guesses came faster.

In the end, the night animals won. Darkness had its place. Winter had its season. The world was not meant to be all light or all dark — it needed both, cycling through the year like breath through a body.

The story is told only during winter months, when the nights are long and the stories are old. It is sacred because it explains the deepest mystery of the world: why summer gives way to winter, why day surrenders to night, and why the cycle never ends.

Children listen with wide eyes. Elders speak the words in the old way, their voices rising and falling with the rhythm of the game. And when the story is finished, everyone knows their place in the world a little better.
story846:
She was young and her name has been forgotten, which is part of the story. She lived in a village where the elders were kind and the children were cruel, as children sometimes are. They mocked her for her quiet ways, for her habit of walking alone at the edge of the village where the forest began.

One evening, after a particularly harsh day of taunting, she walked into the wilderness. She did not take food or water. She did not look back. The trees closed behind her like a curtain.

She walked for three days. On the first day, her hands began to change — her fingers thickening, her nails curving into dark claws. On the second day, fur crept up her arms and across her shoulders, warm and coarse. On the third day, she dropped to all fours and ran.

She was a bear now. Not a woman who had become a bear, but a bear who had once been a woman. The memories were still there, dim and distant, like firelight seen through deep water.

Years later, a hunting party from her old village tracked a great bear to its den. When the lead hunter looked into the bear's eyes, he saw something human there — a recognition, a sadness. "It is her," he whispered. "The one who walked away."

The bear looked at the hunters and did not flee. She turned and walked deeper into the forest, and the hunters let her go.

The story became part of the Mountain Top Chant — the ceremony that heals those who have been touched by animal spirits. When a person falls ill after an encounter with a bear, the medicine man sings the songs the bear woman learned in the wilderness, and the boundary between human and animal is made clear again.

Bear holds great power in Navajo tradition. The bear is not merely an animal but a being who exists on the threshold between the human world and the spirit world. To harm a bear without proper ceremony is to invite transformation — the kind that cannot be reversed.
story847:
The Mountain Top Chant — Dzil Naʼoodilii — began with a girl and a bear, as many sacred things begin with something unexpected.

A young Navajo woman was preparing for her puberty ceremony when she wandered into the high country to gather the materials she would need — pine boughs, sacred corn pollen, the white shell that represented her connection to the East. The mountain air was thin and cold, and the pines stood like sentinels along the ridge.

The bear found her there. It was not the kind of bear that runs from humans. It stood on its hind legs and spoke in a voice like wind through hollow reeds. "I have come to teach you," the bear said. "You will learn songs that heal. You will learn sandpaintings that restore the broken places in people's bodies and spirits."

For seven days, the bear taught her. Each morning, they climbed higher into the mountains. Each night, the bear sang songs that made the stones vibrate and the stars lean closer. The girl learned the nine days of the ceremony — the songs, the prayers, the sandpaintings that map the Holy People's journey through the sacred mountains.

She learned that the sandpaintings are not art but medicine — each line a prayer, each color a direction, each figure a Holy Person who can be called upon to restore balance. The paintings are made on the floor of the healing lodge, and when the ceremony is complete, they are swept away, their power absorbed into the patient.

When she returned to her people, she taught them the ceremony. And so the Mountain Top Chant entered the Navajo healing tradition, used to cure illnesses caused by bears and other animals — the sickness that comes from disturbing a bear's den, from stepping on a bear's track, from encountering a bear in the wrong way at the wrong time.

The ceremony lasts nine days. The medicine man sings hundreds of songs. Sandpaintings appear and disappear like dreams. And when it is over, the patient rises, healed, and walks back into the world carrying a gratitude that extends to the bear who first taught the songs in the high country where the pines stand like sentinels and the air tastes of snow.
story848:
White Bead Maiden — Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ — lived in the Third World before the flood, in a village near the Crossing of the Waters. She was beautiful in the way that white shell is beautiful — pale, luminous, with a light that seemed to come from within rather than from the sun above.

The Sun saw her. From his path across the sky, he watched her walking along the river, her white shell body catching his rays and throwing them back like mirrors. He loved her from that distance, the way one loves a song heard through water — faintly, achingly.

He came to her in human form, a young man wrapped in light so bright she had to shield her eyes. He courted her with gifts of turquoise and eagle feathers. He told her stories of the sky world, where the houses were made of light and the rivers ran with liquid star. After many days, she agreed to marry him.

She traveled to his house in the eastern horizon, where the sun rises each morning. The house was square and beautiful, built of turquoise and white shell, with the four directions marked on its walls. There she bore him twin sons — Monster Slayer and Child of the Water — who would grow up to destroy the monsters of the Fourth World.

But the Sun already had another wife. Jealousy grew in the celestial household like a disease. The other wife whispered against White Bead Maiden, and the Sun, torn between his loves, grew cold.

White Bead Maiden returned to earth. She walked out of the eastern horizon and down the mountain, carrying nothing but her two sons. When she reached the ground, she was no longer White Bead Maiden. She had become Changing Woman — Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé — the woman who changes with the seasons, who ages and renews, who represents the eternal cycle of life.

She settled on the western ocean, where she built a floating house of turquoise and abalone. And from there, she watches over the Navajo people, aging through the winter and reborn each spring, a reminder that even the Sun's love cannot contain the power of a woman who chooses to change.
story849:
After the Hero Twins destroyed the great monsters — Yéʼiitsoh, Déélgééd, the giant birds, the cliff-kicker — four lesser monsters remained. They were not large or fearsome. They did not devour people or destroy villages. They were simply there, crouching at the edges of the world like shadows that would not lift.

Old Age — Są́ — sat in the corner of every dwelling, his breath thin and cold. Cold — Dǫǫh — clung to the bones of the elderly and the exposed. Poverty — Téʼéʼį́ — whispered that there was never enough. Hunger — Báhí — gnawed at the belly even after a full meal.

Monster Slayer found them and raised his lightning arrows. But they did not run. They stood before him, small and trembling, and they spoke.

Old Age said: "If you destroy me, the world will fill with people until there is no room to walk. The old will remain in their prime forever, and the young will never be born. Without me, there is no wisdom, for wisdom comes from the years that aging brings."

Cold said: "If you destroy me, people will forget their mortality. They will take no shelter, make no preparation, waste the gifts of summer. I remind them that comfort is temporary and must be cherished."

Poverty said: "If you destroy me, people will hoard and never share. They will not know the joy of giving, for giving comes from having less than you need. I make the community care for its own."

Hunger said: "If you destroy me, people will eat without gratitude. They will waste food and forget that every meal is a gift. I make them pray before they eat. I make them thank the buffalo and the corn and the rain."

Monster Slayer listened. His brother listened. The arguments were sound. The world required balance — not perpetual joy, but the full range of human experience.

They lowered their weapons. "You may remain," Monster Slayer said, "but only in diminished form. You will trouble the people, but you will not destroy them. You will remind them, but you will not break them."

And so Old Age, Cold, Poverty, and Hunger became part of the natural order — permanent companions to every human life, unwelcome but necessary, like the winter that makes the spring worth celebrating.
story850:
The day came when Changing Woman knew it was time to leave. She was old again — winter old, with white hair and skin like crumpled paper — and she called the Holy People to the shore.

"I am going west," she said. "To a place where the ocean meets the sky, where the sun sleeps at night. I have built a house there — turquoise on the outside, abalone on the inside, white shell for the floor and jet for the door. It floats on the water like a prayer boat, and it will be my home forever."

The people wept. Children clung to her robes. Even the Holy People bowed their heads.

"Do not weep," she told them. "I am not dying. I am going to live forever in a different way. Each year, I will age through the winter, just as I have done here. Each spring, I will be young again. The seasons you see — the fall of leaves, the snow, the first green shoot — these are my breath, my heartbeat, the turning of my body."

She blessed the corn fields, laying her hands on the stalks and whispering prayers that made the ears swell with milk. She blessed the sheep, touching each one on the head. She taught the people the ceremonies they would need — the Blessing Way, the songs of protection and renewal — and gave them the knowledge of how to perform them correctly.

"When you are in trouble," she said, "perform the ceremonies I have taught you. I will hear you from the west, and I will send my blessings on the wind."

She walked into a boat made of light and drifted toward the horizon. The people watched from the shore until she was a speck, then a point of light, then nothing. But the sun set in the place where she had gone, and the colors of the western sky — red and gold and deep purple — are Changing Woman's house, glowing with the light of her fire.

Every autumn, when the leaves turn gold and the wind grows cold, the Navajo know that Changing Woman is aging. Every spring, when the first warm breeze blows from the west and the lambs are born, they know she has been reborn.

She is still there, in her house of turquoise and abalone, watching over the people she loved enough to leave.
